claims.claim: Ouvrage Hackenberg's underground galleries run at an average depth of about thirty meters.
claims.episode_span: French troops at Ouvrage Hackenberg rotated through underground barracks connected by electric railways, confident that concrete positions buried as much as thirty meters deep
claims.supporting_quote: More than 1,200 metres (3,900 ft) of underground galleries connect the entries to the farthest blocks 4 and 5, at an average depth of 30 metres (98 ft)

claims.claim: André Maginot died in Paris on 7 January 1932, of typhoid fever, before the fortification line bearing his name was completed.
claims.episode_span: André Maginot himself toured the sites before his death in 1932
claims.supporting_quote: he became ill in December 1931 and died in Paris on 7 January 1932 of typhoid fever

claims.claim: In 1934 Charles de Gaulle published Vers l'Armée de Métier (Towards a Professional Army), advocating mechanized, professional armored forces.
claims.episode_span: including Colonel Charles de Gaulle, warned in parliamentary hearings and in his 1934 book Vers l'armée de métier that the money would be better spent on mobile armored divisions
claims.supporting_quote: In 1934 de Gaulle wrote Vers l'Armée de Métier ( Towards a Professional Army ). He proposed mechanization of the infantry, with stress on an élite force of 100,000 men and 3,000 tanks.

claims.claim: On 10 May 1940 German armies invaded Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and parts of France, with armoured units advancing through the Ardennes and crossing the Meuse.
claims.episode_span: On 10 May 1940, German Army Group A under Gerd von Rundstedt committed seven panzer divisions to the Ardennes sector
claims.supporting_quote: On 10 May 1940, Wehrmacht armies invaded Belgium , Luxembourg , the Netherlands and parts of France. In Fall Gelb (Case Yellow), German armoured units advanced through the Ardennes , crossed the Meuse and raced down the Somme valley

claims.claim: Gerd von Rundstedt was the commander of German Army Group A, and the breakthrough point at Sedan lay in Army Group A's sector.
claims.episode_span: German Army Group A under Gerd von Rundstedt committed seven panzer divisions to the Ardennes sector
claims.supporting_quote: A breakthrough was needed to encircle and destroy the main body of Allied forces. The most practical place to achieve this would be in the region of Sedan , which lay in the sector of Army Group A.

claims.claim: The German plan for Fall Gelb assigned seven panzer divisions to Army Group A.
claims.episode_span: committed seven panzer divisions to the Ardennes sector that French planners had left covered by only nine second-rate divisions
claims.supporting_quote: He had no intention of allowing an independent strategic penetration by the seven Panzer divisions of Army Group A.

claims.claim: The German assault at Sedan, with its Meuse crossings, took place on 13 May 1940.
claims.episode_span: when the German columns emerged from the forest on 13 May near Sedan, French reserve formations were still positioned hundreds of kilometers to the north
claims.supporting_quote: In the early hours of 13 May, the 10th Panzer Division slipped into position upstream to the north-east of Sedan, ready to strike at its designated crossing point near the town of Wadelincourt

claims.claim: About 1.75 million French soldiers were captured in the Battle of France, consistent with the digest's 'internment of 1.8 million soldiers'.
claims.episode_span: the capture or destruction of nearly all French heavy equipment, the internment of 1.8 million soldiers
claims.supporting_quote: 15,000 missing [ g ] , 1,756,000 captured 1,274 French aircraft lost [ 24 ] 931 British aircraft lost

claims.claim: France signed the Second Armistice at Compiègne with Germany on 22 June 1940, within six weeks of the 10 May offensive.
claims.episode_span: within six weeks of the May 1940 offensive the French government had fled Paris and signed an armistice at Compiègne
claims.supporting_quote: On 22 June 1940, the Second Armistice at Compiègne was signed by France and Germany.
